# Purpose and scope

This vignette documents the scientific and software rationale for `agriGLMflow`.
It is deliberately broader than a feature list. Its purpose is to establish what is
already well solved in the R ecosystem, where the workflow remains fragmented for
agricultural experiments, and which design decisions in `agriGLMflow` follow from
that gap.

The review snapshot is dated **12 August 2026**. The comparison covers major
agriculture-oriented packages, general GLM/GLMM engines, distributional and vector
regression frameworks, and widely used post-model inference and diagnostic tools.
It is a scoped ecosystem review, not a claim that every R package ever published was
screened. Accordingly, the defensible novelty statement is that **within the reviewed
set, no single package was identified that simultaneously provides the complete
combination of design declaration, response characterization, admissible-family
screening, design-compatible engine routing, quantitative-treatment regression,
post-model inference, diagnostics, graphics, reporting, and an auditable decision
trail for agricultural experiments**.

Scientific-reference metadata used in this vignette were checked against two sources.
The verification record is distributed with the package in
`inst/METADATA_VERIFICATION.md` and `inst/metadata/reference_verification.csv`.

# Review strategy

The comparison was assembled from three evidence layers: (1) current CRAN package
indices, manuals, vignettes, and official citation records for software capabilities and
version-dependent restrictions; (2) peer-reviewed software and methodological papers for
the statistical frameworks; and (3) recent comparative or review literature where
available. Packages were selected to represent the principal roles that an agronomic
workflow must connect: agricultural experimental design, GLM/GLMM fitting, distributional
and vector regression, smooth and nonlinear modelling, Bayesian multilevel modelling,
post-model inference, and diagnostics.

This is therefore a **representative, reproducible state-of-the-art comparison**, not an
exhaustive census of CRAN. The comparison date is essential because package capabilities
and versions change. The exact software snapshot is recorded in
`inst/METADATA_VERIFICATION.md`.

# Why generalized modelling requires an agronomic workflow

Agricultural responses frequently violate the assumptions of a Gaussian, independent,
constant-variance response. Examples include insect and disease counts, germination
successes, bounded proportions, ordinal injury scores, positive skewed physiological
measurements, repeated observations from the same plot, and experiments repeated over
environments. Madden and Ojiambo [-@MaddenOjiambo2024] emphasize that moving from LMMs
to GLMMs in plant sciences introduces substantive choices involving conditional versus
marginal interpretation, overdispersion, fitting method, link function, and the response
distribution. These decisions are not cosmetic because they can alter the estimand,
standard errors, and biological interpretation.

At the same time, quantitative treatments should often remain quantitative. Nonlinear
relationships are common in crop and soil processes, and nonlinear regression requires
more than choosing the curve with the largest coefficient of determination
[@ArchontoulisMiguez2015]. This motivates treating design structure, response distribution,
and regression shape as connected parts of the same analysis rather than as separate
software tasks.

# The ecosystem is strong but specialized

The rationale for `agriGLMflow` is **not** that R lacks high-quality modelling tools.
The opposite is true. The ecosystem contains mature packages that solve individual
parts of the problem exceptionally well.

## Agriculture-oriented packages

`AgroR` was developed specifically to facilitate agricultural experiment analysis and
provides experimental-design analyses, assumption checks, multiple comparisons,
graphical outputs, and a Shiny interface [@ShimizuEtAl2025]. It therefore occupies an
important role in accessible agricultural statistics. Its purpose, however, is different
from building a multi-engine distributional modelling layer spanning GLMM, GAMLSS,
VGAM, response-family screening, and a unified audit trail.

`AgroReg` focuses on linear and nonlinear regression for agricultural applications.
This is complementary to `agriGLMflow`: the latter retains quantitative treatments as
quantitative by default but connects curve modelling to non-Gaussian likelihoods,
experimental-unit structure, uncertainty, diagnostics, and downstream inference.
The need for careful nonlinear modelling in agriculture is well established
[@ArchontoulisMiguez2015].

Long-established agricultural-design packages are also central to the ecosystem.
`agricolae` provides extensive planning and analysis functionality for agricultural and
plant-breeding designs, including complete blocks, Latin squares, lattice and alpha
designs, split-plot and strip-plot layouts, multiple-comparison procedures, and selected
multi-location tools. `ExpDes` and `ExpDes.pt` provide compact workflows for CRD/DIC,
RBD/DBC, Latin squares, factorials, split plots, multiple comparisons, residual analyses,
and polynomial regression for quantitative treatments. These packages remain valuable
for classical design-based analyses. `agriGLMflow` does not attempt to replace them.
Instead, it extends the design-first idea to responses and dependence structures that
require generalized, mixed, vector, or distributional models.

## Mixed-model engines

`lme4` is a foundational implementation for linear and generalized linear mixed models
and provides a well-established formula representation for fixed and random effects
[@BatesEtAl2015]. It is used as a reference engine in `agriGLMflow` where its supported
model class is appropriate.

`glmmTMB` greatly expands the GLMM family space and supports, among other extensions,
zero-inflated and flexible count models [@BrooksEtAl2017]. It is therefore the principal
frequentist GLMM backend in `agriGLMflow` when a design requires random effects and the
requested family is supported.

`GLMMadaptive` provides likelihood-based GLMM fitting using adaptive Gaussian quadrature.
Its current implementation permits multiple random-effect terms within **one grouping
factor**, but only one grouping factor. This makes it valuable for compatible grouped
models but prevents using it as a universal replacement for models that require several
experimental-unit grouping factors. `agriGLMflow` encodes this as a routing constraint,
not as a warning that the user must remember manually.

## Distributional regression and GAMLSS

GAMLSS generalized regression beyond the conditional mean by allowing location, scale,
and shape parameters to depend on explanatory variables [@RigbyStasinopoulos2005;
@StasinopoulosEtAl2018]. A recent state-of-the-art primer further frames GAMLSS as a
central distributional-regression approach for modelling variability, quantiles, skewness,
tail behaviour, and exceedance probabilities [@MerderEtAl2026]. This is especially useful
when agricultural treatments alter not only the expected response but also its variability
or distributional shape.

`agriGLMflow` therefore treats GAMLSS as a first-class distributional backend, but does
not pretend that every GAMLSS random-effect construction is interchangeable with every
likelihood-based GLMM. The experimental design remains the first routing constraint.

## VGAM and vector generalized modelling

The VGAM framework extends generalized regression to vector generalized linear and
additive models and has long supported categorical structures such as multinomial and
ordinal models [@Yee2010; @Yee2015]. Current VGAM documentation reports more than 100
models/distributions while also stating a critical limitation: the current implementation
is fixed-effects only. This makes VGAM particularly valuable for multinomial, flexible
ordinal, Dirichlet, Dirichlet-multinomial, simplex, censored, extreme-value, and other
specialized fixed-effects responses, while making it inappropriate for an agronomic design
that requires random block, plot, environment, or subject effects.

`agriGLMflow` uses this limitation constructively: VGAM is available when scientifically
and structurally compatible and is hard-blocked or rerouted when the declared design
requires random effects.

A recent systematic review of ordinal-regression software identified 48 CRAN packages
and described VGAM as the most versatile package in terms of the ordinal model/link
coverage evaluated [@PujolRigolEtAl2025]. The publisher subsequently issued a
[correction](https://doi.org/10.1002/wics.70060) to Table 4 concerning entries for GLMcat
and `brms`; this reinforces why `agriGLMflow` dates its ecosystem comparisons rather
than treating software capabilities as permanent facts.

## Specialized response models

`betareg` established a dedicated regression framework for beta-distributed responses,
including modelling of the precision parameter [@CribariNetoZeileis2010]. Modern versions
also provide extensions for responses that may reach the boundaries of the unit interval.
The package is retained as a specialized engine rather than reproducing its estimator.

`ordinal` provides cumulative-link and cumulative-link mixed models and remains an
important backend when ordered responses require random effects. VGAM complements it with
additional fixed-effects ordinal formulations such as adjacent-category,
continuation-ratio, stopping-ratio, and partial proportional-odds structures.

# Complementary modelling frameworks beyond the frequentist core

The ecosystem also contains broad frameworks that overlap important parts of the
`agriGLMflow` roadmap without eliminating the need for agronomic orchestration. `brms`
provides Bayesian multilevel, nonlinear, zero-inflated, hurdle, ordinal, censored,
multivariate, and distributional models through Stan [@Buerkner2017]. It is consequently
a major advanced backend candidate, but Bayesian prior specification, posterior
diagnostics, computational cost, and posterior-scale inference form a workflow distinct
from the frequentist CRAN 1.0 core. `agriGLMflow` therefore treats Bayesian modelling as
an explicit extension rather than silently mixing inferential paradigms.

`mgcv` is a leading framework for generalized additive and generalized additive mixed
models, with smoothness estimation and distributions extending well beyond elementary
Gaussian regression [@Wood2025]. It is complementary to the package's quantitative
treatment module when the scientific objective is a flexible smooth relationship rather
than a mechanistic or low-dimensional parametric dose-response curve.

Diagnostics are similarly specialized. `DHARMa` supplies simulation-based residual
diagnostics for many hierarchical and generalized models, whereas `hnp` provides
half-normal plots with simulation envelopes for generalized and overdispersed models
[@MoralEtAl2017]. These tools strengthen model checking but do not themselves encode the
agricultural experimental unit or choose a design-compatible probability-model engine.

# Post-model inference and diagnostics are another software layer

Model fitting is only part of an agricultural analysis. Estimated marginal means,
contrasts, treatment-versus-control comparisons, slopes, response-scale predictions, and
diagnostic checks typically require additional packages.

The methodology underlying estimated marginal means and contrasts is documented by
Lenth [-@Lenth2016], and the modern `emmeans` package provides a broad interface for EMMs,
contrasts, trends, and comparisons of slopes. `agriGLMflow` uses `emmeans` where the fitted
model class has validated native support rather than reimplementing that mathematics.

`marginaleffects` provides a general framework for translating fitted models into
predictions, comparisons, slopes, ratios, and other quantities of interest across a wide
range of model classes [@ArelBundockEtAl2024]. `agriGLMflow` uses this layer selectively
when it improves interpretation while retaining agronomic design semantics.

`performance` provides a consistent toolbox for model-quality assessment and checks such
as overdispersion, zero inflation, singularity, and related diagnostics across many model
classes [@LudeckeEtAl2021]. Simulation-based diagnostics such as those provided by DHARMa
are additionally useful for many GLM/GLMM classes. These packages address model checking;
they do not define the agricultural experimental unit or decide which engine can validly
represent a split-plot or multi-environment structure.

# Comparative capability matrix

The following matrix describes the **primary scope** of the reviewed packages rather than
ranking their statistical quality. "Primary" means that the capability is central to the
package; "available" means it is supported but is not the package's defining role;
"specialized" indicates an intentionally narrower scope; and "orchestrated" denotes a
capability that `agriGLMflow` coordinates through validated backends.

| Package/framework | Primary role | Agricultural design semantics | Mixed/random effects | Broad or specialized distribution families | Multiparameter distributional modelling | Multinomial/compositional | Quantitative nonlinear regression | Post-model inference | Unified audit/routing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **agricolae** | Agricultural design/planning and analysis | **Primary** | Selected classical/mixed-analysis tools | Classical agricultural procedures | Not primary | Not primary | Selected regression tools | Multiple comparisons | No |
| **ExpDes / ExpDes.pt** | Classical experimental-design analysis | **Primary** | Classical design strata | Mostly ANOVA-oriented | Not primary | No | Polynomial/nonlinear utilities | Multiple comparisons | No |
| **AgroR** | Agricultural experiment analysis | **Primary** | Available for selected workflows | Selected GLM/mixed workflows | Not primary | Not primary | Available for agricultural analyses | Multiple comparisons | Not its primary purpose |
| **AgroReg** | Agricultural regression | Limited | Not primary | Regression-focused | Not primary | Not primary | **Primary** | Regression summaries | No |
| **lme4** | LMM/GLMM engine | Formula-based, not agronomy-specific | **Primary** | Conventional mixed-model families | No | No | Limited | Via other packages | No |
| **glmmTMB** | Extended GLMM engine | Formula-based, not agronomy-specific | **Primary** | **Primary, broad GLMM families** | Dispersion/ZI components available | Limited | Covariate regression within GLMM | Via other packages | No |
| **GLMMadaptive** | Adaptive-quadrature GLMM | Not agronomy-specific | **Specialized: one grouping factor** | Selected GLMM families | Selected extensions | Selected ordinal/ZI extensions | Covariate regression | Package/other tools | No |
| **GAMLSS** | Distributional regression | Not agronomy-specific | Specialized random-effect mechanisms | **Very broad** | **Primary** | Selected families | Smooth/nonlinear terms | GAMLSS ecosystem | No |
| **VGAM** | VGLM/VGAM | Not agronomy-specific | **No in current VGAM** | **Very broad fixed-effect families** | **Primary for many VGLMs** | **Primary strength** | VGAM smoothers | Requires class-specific handling | No |
| **betareg** | Beta/extended beta regression | No | No general mixed-effects engine | **Specialized** | Mean/precision structures | No | Covariate regression | Via supported tools | No |
| **ordinal** | Ordinal CLM/CLMM | No | **Available in CLMM** | Ordinal only | Threshold/scale structures | Ordinal, not nominal composition | Covariate regression | Via supported tools | No |
| **brms** | Bayesian multilevel/distributional modelling | Formula-based, not agronomy-specific | **Primary** | **Broad Bayesian family support** | **Primary** | Multivariate/ordinal supported | Nonlinear/smooth terms | Posterior inference | No agronomic router |
| **mgcv** | GAM/GAMM and smooth regression | Formula-based, not agronomy-specific | Available through GAMM/random-effect smooths | Broad GAM families | Selected location-scale/general families | Selected multivariate/general families | **Primary smooth modelling** | Model-specific | No agronomic router |
| **DHARMa** | Simulation-based residual diagnostics | Consumes fitted model | Model dependent | Not a fitting engine | Not a fitting engine | Model dependent | No | Diagnostic layer | No |
| **hnp** | Half-normal simulation envelopes | Consumes fitted model | Model dependent | Diagnostic support across fitted classes | Not a fitting engine | Model dependent | No | Diagnostic layer | No |
| **emmeans** | EMMs, contrasts, trends | Consumes fitted model | Not a fitting engine | Not a fitting engine | Not a fitting engine | Class dependent | Trends/slopes post fit | **Primary** | No |
| **marginaleffects** | Predictions, comparisons, slopes | Consumes fitted model | Model dependent | Model dependent | Model dependent | Model dependent | Post-fit slopes/effects | **Primary** | No |
| **performance** | Model assessment/diagnostics | Consumes fitted model | Model dependent | Model dependent | Model dependent | Model dependent | No | Diagnostic layer | No |
| **agriGLMflow** | Agronomic modelling orchestrator | **Primary** | **Routes to compatible engines** | **Registry across engines** | **Routes GAMLSS/VGAM/other engines** | **Routes VGAM/ordinal-compatible paths** | **Integrated** | **Integrated** | **Primary** |

This table is intentionally asymmetric. Mature specialist packages should remain
specialists. The proposed contribution of `agriGLMflow` is to preserve their strengths
while supplying the design-aware connective tissue between them.

# The gap addressed by agriGLMflow

The reviewed ecosystem suggests five distinct layers:

1. **Experimental design.** Agricultural software is strongest when the user specifies
   DIC/CRD, RCBD, factorial, split-plot, repeated, or related structures explicitly.
2. **Probability model.** General statistical engines provide deeper family and dependence
   support than a single agriculture-oriented package can reasonably reimplement.
3. **Distributional/vector extensions.** GAMLSS and VGAM cover different but complementary
   model spaces.
4. **Post-model inference.** EMMs, contrasts, predictions, and marginal effects are handled
   by dedicated infrastructure.
5. **Diagnostics and validation.** Model checking is itself a multi-package task.

The practical gap is therefore not the absence of algorithms. It is the need to move
reliably between these layers **without losing the experimental unit, response support,
interpretation scale, or decision history**.

`agriGLMflow` addresses that gap through the following sequence:

```text
experimental design
        -> response characterization
        -> scientifically admissible family set
        -> design-compatible engine routing
        -> convergence and diagnostic gates
        -> model comparison within the admissible set
        -> post-model inference / quantitative regression
        -> prediction and graphics
        -> reproducible report + audit trail
```

# Why agriGLMflow is not simply a wrapper

A thin wrapper merely renames another package's function. The intended scientific
contribution here is different.

## 1. The design can veto the engine

If a split-plot requires whole-plot and subplot experimental units, a backend that cannot
represent both is rejected. The design is not simplified to make software execution easier.
The same principle applies to split-split, strip-plot, repeated-measures, and
multi-environment structures.

## 2. Family screening is constrained by support and diagnostics

The candidate set begins with the mathematical support and scientific process of the
response. A model that has a smaller AIC but fails convergence, residual, dispersion, or
structural checks does not automatically become the recommended model.

## 3. Engines are capabilities, not identities

`glmmTMB`, GAMLSS, VGAM, `ordinal`, `betareg`, `brglm2`, `lme4`, and
`GLMMadaptive` solve different statistical problems. The router records why an engine was
selected and why alternatives were rejected.

## 4. Agronomic quantitative regression remains connected to the likelihood model

Dose, rate, time, and density variables remain numeric by default. Linear, polynomial,
plateau, mechanistic, nonlinear, or smooth relationships are considered without discarding
the non-Gaussian response or experimental-unit structure.

## 5. The audit trail is part of the statistical result

`agri_audit()` records design requirements, family candidates, engine decisions,
convergence/diagnostic outcomes, inferential scale, and post-model choices. This is intended
to make automated assistance inspectable rather than opaque.

# What agriGLMflow deliberately does not claim

The package does **not** claim that one automatic algorithm can identify the true
probability distribution in every experiment. It does not claim that the lowest AIC is
scientific proof. It does not replace the statistical engines it calls, and it does not
make specialist packages obsolete.

Its stronger and more defensible claim is that an agricultural workflow can make the
constraints linking **design, distribution, dependence, engine capability, diagnostics,
and interpretation explicit and reproducible**.

The current development snapshot still requires runtime validation with R and all optional
backends before a CRAN release. The planned simulation programme therefore evaluates
parameter recovery, interval coverage, type-I error, power, convergence, family-set
recovery, diagnostic sensitivity/specificity, and predictive calibration rather than
validating the workflow only through software examples.

# Reproducible metadata policy

Scientific metadata in this vignette are stored in `vignettes/references.bib`. Each DOI is
also listed in `inst/metadata/reference_verification.csv`, together with two sources used to
check author, title, year, outlet, volume/issue/pages or article number, and DOI. The human-
readable verification notes are in `inst/METADATA_VERIFICATION.md`.

Package versions are inherently time-dependent. Version numbers in the verification notes
therefore describe the **12 August 2026 snapshot** and should be refreshed before a journal
submission or CRAN release.
